prompt: What is the difference between a HIDS and a HIPS?

choices.text: A HIDS runs on servers and a HIPS on workstations
choices.why: Both run on any host.

choices.text: A HIPS watches the network and a HIDS watches files
choices.why: Both watch the host; they differ in what they do next.

choices.text: A HIDS alerts; a HIPS acts on its own
choices.why: Right: two settings of one dial.

choices.text: A HIPS needs a kernel module and a HIDS does not
choices.why: fail2ban is a HIPS made of a log reader and a firewall rule.

prompt: When does a rule belong on the prevention side?

choices.text: When it is never wrong
choices.why: Right: a wrong block costs far more than a wrong alert.

choices.text: When the threat it describes is serious enough to justify it
choices.why: A serious rule that is sometimes wrong locks people out of serious work.

choices.text: When nobody is available to read alerts at night
choices.why: Staffing does not make a rule more certain.

choices.text: Whenever the product supports blocking for that rule
choices.why: Supporting it is not the same as being right.

prompt: Match each tool to what it does in this lesson.

pairs.right: bans an address after repeated failed logins
reports files changed since an approved state
confines a program to what it may touch

prompt: fail2ban-client lists desk as banned. What still has to be checked?

choices.text: That desk's address is written in jail.local
choices.why: Addresses are learnt from the log, not written in the jail.

choices.text: That desk is actually refused on port 22
choices.why: Right: a ban whose action failed is still listed.

choices.text: That the portal on port 80 has stopped answering desk too
choices.why: multiport bans only the jail's ports; port 80 should keep answering.

choices.text: That AIDE recorded the ban in its database
choices.why: AIDE watches files, not bans.

prompt: Why does the lesson write jail.local instead of editing jail.conf?

choices.text: Because jail.conf is read-only for root
choices.why: Root can edit it; it should not.

choices.text: Because fail2ban ignores jail.conf on Ubuntu
choices.why: It reads it first, then jail.local over it.

choices.text: Because jail.local is the only file that may enable a jail
choices.why: Ubuntu's own file in jail.d enables the sshd jail.

choices.text: The package's own file stays untouched for updates
choices.why: Right: jail.local overrides it.

prompt: While desk was banned, why did the portal on port 80 still answer it?

choices.text: The ban rule matches port 22 only
choices.why: Right: the jail's ports, and nothing else.

choices.text: Because nginx is exempt from every nftables rule
choices.why: Nothing exempts nginx; the rule names port 22.

choices.text: Because HTTP connections are never banned by fail2ban
choices.why: A jail for a web server would ban on port 80.

choices.text: Because the ban had already expired by then
choices.why: The ban was ten minutes; both checks were seconds apart.

prompt: How many failures did Ubuntu's own sshd jail allow before a ban, before jail.local changed it?
Why does the lesson move portal.db.new into place by hand instead of letting AIDE do it?

choices.text: Because AIDE cannot overwrite its own files
choices.why: It could; the separation is deliberate.

choices.text: Moving it is a person approving that state
choices.why: Right: a database built on a changed machine approves the change.

choices.text: To save disk space by keeping one database only
choices.why: Space is not the reason.

choices.text: Because the check refuses a database younger than a day
choices.why: No such rule; the check ran at once.

prompt: AIDE reports /opt/portal/backup.sh as changed. What does that report establish?

choices.text: That an intruder edited the script
choices.why: It cannot tell an intruder's edit from an administrator's.

choices.text: That the script will fail the next time root runs it
choices.why: AIDE knows nothing about whether it works.

choices.text: Only that it differs from the approved state
choices.why: Right: a person decides whether the change was right.

choices.text: That its permissions were changed to world-writable
choices.why: The report showed size and hash, not permissions.

prompt: Why should the nightly AIDE report be sent off the machine?

choices.text: Because AIDE cannot write reports to local disk
choices.why: It writes to stdout or a file without trouble.

choices.text: Whoever altered the server would alter a local report too
choices.why: Right: lesson 8's argument about telemetry.

choices.text: To save the time it takes to read it on the server
choices.why: Time is not the argument.

choices.text: Because the law requires integrity reports to be kept elsewhere
choices.why: No such requirement was cited.

prompt: The portal runs as root. What can an AppArmor profile for it still prevent?

choices.text: Anything outside its profile, root or not
choices.why: Right: confinement is about the program, not the account.

choices.text: Nothing: root bypasses every access control
choices.why: Mandatory access control applies to root too.

choices.text: Only reading files in /home, which root never needs
choices.why: A profile lists whatever the program may touch.

choices.text: Only network connections to other machines
choices.why: Files, network and capabilities can all be confined.

prompt: Match each mode to what it does.

pairs.right: logs what the profile would refuse
refuses what the profile does not allow

prompt: Why could this lesson not run AppArmor inside web?

choices.text: Because AppArmor only exists on Red Hat systems
choices.why: AppArmor is Ubuntu's default; Red Hat uses SELinux.

choices.text: Its policy is the shared kernel's, which only the host loads
choices.why: Right: in your own VM, outside the containers, it runs.

choices.text: Because the portal is written in Python
choices.why: Python programs are confined like any other.

choices.text: Because profiles need a licence the course does not have
choices.why: AppArmor is free software.

prompt: What does adding admin to ignoreip protect against, and what does it cost?

choices.text: It protects web from admin; it costs nothing
choices.why: It does the opposite: admin is never banned.

choices.text: Locking out the administrators; an intruder on admin is never banned
choices.why: Right: which is why admin machines are the best protected.

choices.text: Password guessing from admin; it costs a longer bantime
choices.why: ignoreip stops bans, it does not stop guessing.

choices.text: Log flooding; it costs the jail's whole log
choices.why: Failures from admin are still logged.

prompt: A server reachable from the internet shows a total of 0 failed logins in its sshd jail after three months. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Nobody has tried to log in
choices.why: Every server on the internet sees attempts within hours.

choices.text: The bantime is so long that every attacker gave up
choices.why: Failures are counted before any ban.

choices.text: The jail is reading a log that no longer receives the lines
choices.why: Right: it counts nothing and bans nobody, quietly.

choices.text: The firewall drops attackers before sshd logs anything
choices.why: Possible only if SSH is closed to the internet, which the question rules out.

prompt: With findtime = 10m and maxretry = 3, how many minutes must a slow guesser wait between attempts so the count never reaches 3? Give the smallest whole number that works.
hint: Two attempts may fall inside one window; the third must not.

prompt: Windows account lockout counts failures per account. What risk does that bring that fail2ban does not have?

choices.text: Guessers on many addresses are never noticed
choices.why: Counting per account notices them wherever they come from.

choices.text: Knowing a name is enough to lock its owner out
choices.why: Right: which is why the threshold is not set low.

choices.text: It bans the domain controller's address
choices.why: It locks accounts, not addresses.

choices.text: It cannot be configured by Group Policy
choices.why: It is a Group Policy setting.

prompt: How does Microsoft advise switching on an attack surface reduction rule?

choices.text: In block mode on every machine on the same day
choices.why: That is how a rule gets switched off by the third week.

choices.text: Only on servers, never on workstations
choices.why: Several rules are aimed at workstations' Office applications.

choices.text: In audit mode first, then block where nothing legitimate appears
choices.why: Right: the same order as this lesson's.

choices.text: After disabling Defender's antivirus, which conflicts with it
choices.why: They are parts of the same product.

prompt: Put the path from a failed login to a refused connection in order.
items: sshd writes the failure to the journal
the jail counts it within findtime
the action adds the address to the nftables set

prompt: Which of these did this lesson show to be checked, not assumed? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: That a listed ban refuses the address
choices.why: nc from desk was refused.

choices.text: That the integrity database is the approved one
choices.why: Approval is moving it into place.

choices.text: That fail2ban's filter understands the sshd log format
choices.why: It counted the failures as they came; the lesson did not need to check it.

choices.text: That the jail is still reading a log that gets lines
choices.why: A silent jail counts nothing.
